content:
As published, con-leche handles nested inductives by building a Lean model of it (untrusted code, including propositional proofs of iota rules), and then the verified “model installer” checks that this is indeed a model of the given inductive and allows its use. This is fine for consistency, and it is rather close to what the official kernel does as well (create a non-nested mutual inductive in its place), only “better” (it also proves that it really is a good model).

But it is still not satisfying, it would be more elegant if we could just run a few checks on the given inductive, and then accept it as it is. I have been working on that for a while now, with some dead end and some successes. I’m in the processes to cleaning it up a bit and plan to merge it eventually, but maybe it’s interesting for someone if I share what I tried so far.

In con-leche, the model of a simple inductive is a fixpoint of a monotone operator. For example, List α is modeleld as L(α)=μ l.1+(α,l)=μ l.CL(α,l)L(α) = \mu\,l. 1 + (α, l) = \mu\,l. C_L(α,l) L(α)=μl.1+(α,l)=μl.CL​(α,l). This is a good definition as long as l↦CL(α,l)l \mapsto C_L(α,l)l↦CL​(α,l) is monotone, which is provided by the positivity check. (There are more requirements to make sure it ends up in the right universe, but I’ll ignore that for this post).

So what do we do with a nested inductive like Rose ::= Unit | List Rose (excuse my short hand syntax. And I throw in the unit just that the operator is a bit less trivial, helps readability)? There are two obvious ways to model this:

Two approaches

Nested fixpoints

R=μ r.CR(r)whereCR(r)=1+L(r)=1+(μ l.CL(r,l))R = \mu\,r. C_R(r) \quad \text{where}\quad C_R(r) =1 + L(r) = 1 + (\mu\,l. C_L(r,l))R=μr.CR​(r)whereCR​(r)=1+L(r)=1+(μl.CL​(r,l))

This is maybe the most direct route: The operator for Rose is in terms of List, we get nested fixpoints that match the nesting of inductives. The positivity check has to decide when L is positive.

Flat fixpoints

R=μ ⟨r,lr⟩.⟨1+lr,CL(r,lr)⟩1R = \mu\,\langle r, lr\rangle. \langle 1 + lr, C_L(r, lr)\rangle_1R=μ⟨r,lr⟩.⟨1+lr,CL​(r,lr)⟩1​

This expands the container inductives to form one big flat wide mutual inductive. If we nest through nested inductives, this expansion is repeated.

This is effectively what the official kernel does.

First attempts

I first tried to go the flat route and verify a copy of the official algorithm.

In theory it’s easy: Every nested inductive gets expanded this way; the ListRose copy of List Rose in the wider fixpoint for Rose can be proven to be equal to the fixpoint of List with a parameter of Rose (by judicous applications of Bekić's theorem).

But in practice, it turned out to be too hard. I think what makes it hard is

  • Highly non-trivial bookkeeping that the proof as to go through.
  • During expansion and positivity checking, the kernel runs whnf here and there. But that means we have to know things like “whnf at the install time of List and whnf at the install time of Rose are related” or “whnf at List α is related to whnf at List Rose”, which gets us dangerously close to the kind of meta-theoretical issue that are lacking in Lean (subject reduction, unique typing, etc.)

(Maybe I should give it another shot now that I learned some more in the process, though.)

Better success

I had better success when I aimed for a positivity check that checks what needs to be checked for th nested fixpoint route to go through. Still a large, tedious proof over a not very small checker code with lots of book keeping, but at least it finished.

Note that positivity isn’t done abstractly (“List is positive in α”) but has to be re-checked at whatever instantiation you come across, a type maybe positive in one parameter if the other one is fun _ => Nat but not if it is fun a => a or so.

Recursors

But even if we can model the inductive that way, we still have to deal with the recursor. The recursor is generated by the official kernel in way that

  • is closely tied to the flat view
  • falls out of official’s particular way of building that flat view

So if we check inductives one way (positivity check), it would be disappointing if we had to re-run all of official’s construction to get the recursor

For a while I was hoping for a very elegant, general, easy approach: Build the inductives in that way, and then check recursors very generally by simply acceping all primitive recursive families of functions (the “interface” for recursors could just as well be one for that). This would be beatiful: We decouple the inductive handling from the code for accepting concrete recursors, we can easily handle whatever recursor shape happens to be in the input, and maybe really support primitive recursors at some point.

For Type this is actually easy in con-leche: We model types and values with sets, fields are ∈-below the constructor, and sets are regular (no infinite descent on ∈), so termination of a primitively recursive function just falls out of that.

But (as always) Prop is the problem: here the model is either ∅\emptyset∅ or {∙}\{\bullet\}{∙}, and no such argument exists. I tried for a while to get a construction here that works, by nested induction, but in that generality I couldn’t do it.

So I scaled back my ambitions, and now it’s only accepting recursors that could be the recursor for the given inductive type. There is still the short-cut that instead of re-running officials algorithm to find the auxiliary types and their order, I read that off the given recursor, do a bunch of checks that relate that to the positivity check done for the nested fixpoint, and construct the recursor I expect and do a defeq check against the given. It seems easier to prove the generation to be good than to verify the code that checks everything about the given recursor, and by doing the final check using defeq we hopefully don’t fall over the moment the official kernel changes something about its generation (e.g. a whnf more or less here or there).

TL;DR

So TL;DR: Do a positivity check, recursively exploring the container inductives at the given instantiation; the nconstruct a recursor based on the shape given in the input.

Or: The theory of nested inductives isn’t absent, or particularly surprising from a theoretical point of view, it’s mostly just very tedious.

I’m still cleaning up what I have, and trying to make the checker algorithm more elegant, then I plan to merge this into con-leche and con-ron. The whole inductive-models training wheel is gone then.

Note that positivity isn’t done abstractly (“α is positive in List”) but has to be re-checked at whatever instantiation you come across, a type maybe positive in one parameter if the other one is fun _ => Nat but not if it is fun a => a or so.

A static under approximation of this such as the "strictly positive parameters" criteria presented in the nested paper would probably cover all existing code ran by users. Ignoring the fact this would mean con-leche wouldn't accept all the things the core kernel currently does, would doing things that way make the formalization any easier ?
@Joachim Breitner Are you planning to integrate this into lean4lean ?

Lean4lean aims to verify the official kernel, so the constraints are different. I also don't expect that anything I write here is new for Mario.
(Just posting it ins this channel because I think Mario indended this to be the place for all kernel verification work, not just lean4lean itself)

Arthur Adjedj schrieb:

Ignoring the fact this would mean con-leche wouldn't accept all the things the core kernel currently does, would doing things that way make the formalization any easier ?

I would expect it would, because then the once established positivity should just transfer over to the instantiations. It would also simplify the checker code itself.

How Claude describes the latest checking of inductives in con-leche

How con-leche checks a block of (possibly mutual, possibly nested) inductive types

Input: the type formers T₁ … Tₖ, their constructors, and the recursors, as exported.
Terms: whnf = reduce to weak-head normal form; defeq = definitionally equal; a hole is a fresh local variable that replaces the constant of a type still being defined. It keeps that type's arguments: Tₘ params indices becomes Xₘ params indices.

1. Type formers

  • Type-check each Tₘ; its type must be Π (params) (indices) → Sort s.
  • All formers share the same parameters (up to defeq) and the same sort s.
  • Add the formers to the environment.

2. Constructors, as declared

  • Type-check each constructor c of Tₘ; its type must be Π params (fields) → Tₘ params indices, with the block's parameters.
  • Every field's sort must fit in s (with the usual exception for Prop blocks that eliminate into Type).

3. Positivity: walk every constructor, and every container it goes through

  • Replace each constant Tₘ by a hole Xₘ (so an occurrence Tₘ params indices becomes Xₘ params indices), then run walk constructors on the block's own constructors.
  • Afterwards: every hole Xₘ occurs applied to exactly the block's parameters, never to anything else (uniform parameters).

Walk constructors (given constructors and their holes). For each constructor:
1. Type-check it with the holes in place.
2. Check each field (below).
3. No later field, and not the result, may depend on the value of a recursive field.
4. The result is headed by a hole, with indices that mention no hole.
5. Remember the constructor's normalised field types (used in step 5).

Check a field e: let w := whnf e.
* w mentions no hole and no Tₘ → fine (a plain field).
* w = Π (a : A), B → A must mention no hole; check B.
* w = H params indices, where H is a hole, params are that hole's parameters (the block's, or the container instance's args), and the indices are hole-free → fine (a recursive field).
* w = C args indices with C an already-installed inductive type, i.e. the recursion is nested through the container C → require that
* the indices mention no hole,
* C's sort is s,
* C's index types (at args) mention no hole;

then walk the container C args.
* Otherwise → reject ("non-positive occurrence").

Walk a container C args:
* If C args is already being walked further up → reject (it was produced by reduction, not written in the declaration).
* If C args was walked before and args mention no hole → done.
* Take C's whole mutual group and replace each of its type constants by a new hole (applied to args wherever the constant was).
* Instantiate the group's stored constructors at args. For example, List's constructors become those of List Rose: the constant List becomes a hole Y, so the recursive field reads Y (X_Rose).
* Walk constructors on those, with the new holes.

4. Large elimination

  • Decide, as official does, whether the recursor may eliminate into Type (for a Prop block: at most one constructor, whose fields are proofs or appear in the result's indices).
  • Add the constructors to the environment.

5. Recursors: generated, not checked

  • Type-check the exported recursor types. Read off them the list of classes, the types the recursors eliminate. This reading is unchecked and only tells us where to look. The classes are the block's own types, plus one auxiliary class per container instance such as List Rose.
  • For each class:
    • it is either one of the Tₘ at the block's parameters, or an installed inductive applied to arguments that mention one of the Tₘ;
    • make sure step 3 walked it (walk it now if not);
    • its constructors are the ones remembered in step 3 for that instance;
    • its recursive fields are the fields whose type mentions a Tₘ.
  • Generate the recursor family exactly as official would, from these classes and constructors:
    • one motive per class;
    • one minor premise per constructor, with an induction hypothesis per recursive field;
    • one recursor per class;
    • one computation rule per constructor.
  • Each generated recursor type must be defeq to the exported one.
  • Install our generated recursors and rules. The exported rules are not read.

Not shown: bookkeeping that exists only so the proof can read the facts back (normalised field types read back with the holes turned into constants, a check that all walked instances of the same class agree, caches, fuel), plus level bookkeeping and structure projections.

How Claude describes the latest checking of inductives in con-leche

How con-leche checks a block of (possibly mutual, possibly nested) inductive types

Input: the type formers T₁ … Tₖ, their constructors, and the recursors, as exported.
Terms: whnf = reduce to weak-head normal form; defeq = definitionally equal. A hole is a fresh local variable that stands for a whole application Tₘ params of a type still being defined. It takes only the indices: Tₘ params indices becomes Xₘ indices.

1. Type formers

  • Type-check each Tₘ; its type must be Π (params) (indices) → Sort s.
  • All formers share the same parameters (up to defeq) and the same sort s.
  • Add them to the environment.

2. Constructors, as declared

  • Type-check each constructor c of Tₘ; its type must be Π params (fields) → Tₘ params indices, at the block's parameters and universe levels.
  • Every field's sort must fit in s (for a Prop block with large elimination: every field is a proof or appears in the result's indices).
  • Parameters must be uniform, syntactically (as in the official kernel): every occurrence of a Tₘ is literally Tₘ params, and no parameter's type mentions a Tₘ.

3. The classes

  • An unchecked pre-pass reads the list of classes off the exported recursor types. These are the types the recursors eliminate: the block's own Tₘ, plus auxiliary ones such as List Rose. The pre-pass only tells us where to look.
  • Each class must be one of the Tₘ at the block's parameters, or an installed inductive (not Quot) whose arguments mention a Tₘ and nothing but parameters. Its sort must be s.

4. Positivity: walk every class

  • Walk the block's own constructors, with each Tₘ params replaced by its hole Xₘ, then walk every other class as a container. Walks share a cache.

Walk constructors (given constructors and their holes). For each constructor:
1. Type-check it with the holes in place.
2. Check each field (below).
3. No later field, and not the result, may depend on the value of a recursive or nested field.
4. The result is a hole applied to hole-free indices.
5. Remember the constructor's normalised field types (used in step 5).

Check a field e: let w := whnf e.
* w mentions no hole and no Tₘ → fine (a plain field).
* w = Π (a : A), B → A must mention no hole; check B.
* w = H indices, with H a hole and hole-free indices → fine (a recursive field).
* w = C args indices, with C an installed inductive (not Quot), fully applied at the right number of universe levels → the recursion is nested through C. Require that:
* args mention no local variables other than parameters and holes;
* the indices mention no hole;
* C's sort is s;
* C's index types (at args) mention no hole.

Then walk the container C args.
* Otherwise → reject ("non-positive occurrence").

Walk a container C args:
* If C args is already being walked further up → reject (it arose by reduction, not from the declaration).
* If it was walked before and args mention no container hole → done.
* Take C's whole mutual group. In each group constructor's stored type, replace every Cⱼ params by a new hole Yⱼ (a family over Cⱼ's indices), then instantiate the parameters at args. For example, List's constructors at List Rose become nil : Y and cons : X_Rose → Y → Y.
* Walk constructors on those, with the new holes.

5. Recursors: generated, not checked

  • Add the constructors to the environment.
  • The exported recursor types are type-checked. Whether they eliminate into Type (large elimination) is read off them and checked: for a block that may be a Prop, this requires one member with at most one constructor and no auxiliary class.
  • For each class and each of its constructors (as remembered in step 4 for that instance):
    • its recursive fields are the fields whose type mentions a Tₘ;
    • the exported minor premise must have exactly one induction hypothesis per recursive field.
  • Generate the recursor family the way the official kernel does, for these classes: one motive per class, one minor premise per constructor (an induction hypothesis per recursive field), one recursor per class, one computation rule per constructor.
  • Each generated recursor type must be defeq to the exported one.
  • Install our generated recursors and rules. The exported rules are never read.

Differences from the official kernel (all sound):
* Nested occurrences equal only up to reduction (e.g. List (id T) next to List T) are identified; official treats them as different auxiliary types.
* Because the classes are read from the input, renamed or extra auxiliary recursors are accepted, and so are any exported rules.
* Sort u families may eliminate into any sort.
* A non-uniform occurrence that exists only inside a let (which the stored type inlines) is not seen.

Not shown: bookkeeping that exists only so the proof can read the facts back (field types read back with each hole as the application it stands for, a check that all walked instances of the same class agree, caches, fuel), and structure projections.

For context, one of the things that the paper doesn't cover, which @Arthur Adjedj informed me of, includes

inductive Higher (f : Type → Type) (α : Type) where
  | mk : f α → Higher f α

set_option genSizeOf false in
inductive Foo where
  | mk : Higher List Foo → Foo

/--
error: (kernel) arg #1 of '_nested.Higher_1.mk' has a non positive occurrence of the datatypes being declared
-/
#guard_msgs in
inductive Bar where
  | mk : Higher (· → Bool) Bar → Bar

That and types hidden behind e.g structures, which @Robin Arnez informed me of, includes

structure Thing where
  type : Type

inductive Test (x : Thing) where
  | none
  | some (value : x.type)

set_option genSizeOf false
inductive Test2 where
  | nest (x : Test { type := Test2 })
well any kind of reduction, isn't it?

Yes, this kind of reduction nonsense also happens in non-mutuals like

inductive Hack where
  | mk : (a : Hack) → (fun _ : Hack => Nat) a → Hack
In metalean, which follows the subtle details of dybjer more faithfully, this sort of thing is unrepresentable

Some more nonsense for the record:

def Set.{u} (α : Sort u) := α → Prop

inductive Foo : Set Nat where
  | mk : Foo 0

which is present in mathlib, but this is already defeq abuse of Set
This juts landed in con-leche master BTW.
Nice. Unfortunately nesteds are not so easy on the type theory side :(
You can't just add extensionality to your theory and use the modelling route, as a first step?

An alternative that I would consider is structural typing for mutual inductives, and then desugaring all nested to mutual the way the official kernel does (the flat wide route). But yeah, if it were easy we'd have had it for years already.

Joachim Breitner said:

You can't just add extensionality to your theory and use the modelling route, as a first step?

I don't think the domain model used in MetaLean works on extensional TTs

It definitely does not: ETT satisfies that in an inconsistent context everything is equal and thus every term is typable. Since in the model ⊥\bot⊥ is inhabited, every context is inconsistent and thus everything should be always equal, which is of course not true. So I think there's a rather strong limitation to using this sort of models to obtain results on extensional type theories.
Could you verify the consistency of nested inductives after the domain model and before the set theoretic model? (Though I imagine that is ugly.)
You certainly can. Just that the size of your code multiplies by two as you now define two type theories
What I intend to do in metalean is just do the nested paper, with some modifications for proof elegance (biting the intrinsics cookie)
Is it possible to test in metacode whether an inductive type is nested/mutual?

metakuntyyy said:

Is it possible to test in metacode whether an inductive type is nested/mutual?

Yes

import Lean.Meta.Basic
open Lean Meta

def nested (name : Name) : MetaM Unit := do
  let info ← getConstInfoInduct name
  println! info.isNested
  println! info.all.length

#eval nested ``Lean.Syntax
